title: Positional roles moderate pattern recall accuracy under varying task complexity in female soccer players.
abstract: In soccer, the ability to rapidly and accurately encode the positions and movement intentions of teammates and opponents is fundamental to effective decision-making. This cognitive skill is underpinned by pattern recall. Extending prior research using complex scene paradigms, this study employed a graded pattern recall task requiring the recall of 2, 4, or 6 players. Two experiments were conducted to examine how task complexity and positional roles moderate recall accuracy in female soccer players. Experiment 1 compared elite (n = 49) and novice (n = 49) players, revealing that elite players demonstrated superior recall accuracy across all levels of task complexity, despite a general decline in performance as the number of to-be-recalled players increased. Experiment 2 further investigated positional differences among elite players (N = 141), including forwards, midfielders, defenders, and wide players. Results showed that forwards and midfielders significantly outperformed defenders and wide players in recall accuracy. These findings indicate that superior pattern recall is not solely a function of general soccer expertise, but is modulated by domain-specific knowledge structures associated with distinct positional roles. This work extends Long-Term Working Memory theory by demonstrating that cognitive advantages in experts are role-dependent and robust against variations in task complexity.
